title: Coding Inequality: How the Use of Big Data Reduces, Obscures, and Amplifies Inequalities
geography: United States (Los Angeles, New York, Oakland)
thesis: Big data policing amplifies and obscures inequality through biased training data, feedback loops, secondary surveillance networks, and system avoidance, despite potential for accountability.
theme_1_justification: Substantive engagement with dual-use potential: discusses repurposing civilian data tools (AVLs, Palantir) for police accountability, and civilian surveillance tools being used to monitor police. However, focus is on police-civilian rather than military-civilian transfer. Explicitly mentions data as 'capital' and transactional, but not specifically on near-zero marginal cost.
theme_2_justification: Substantive engagement with algorithmic opacity: discusses 'black box algorithms' (p. 105), trade secrecy of predictive policing algorithms (p. 117), and hidden feedback loops (p. 107-109). Addresses epistemic authority via 'aura of objectivity' (p. 100) and 'patina of objectivity' (p. 109). Mentions bias in training data and human discretion.
theme_3_justification: Substantive engagement with modulation: discusses predictive policing as continuous modulation of urban populations (points system, place-based algorithms), automated decision-making (TEAMS II, heuristic scores), and real-time tracking (AVLs, ALPRs). Engages with 'smart city' governance via data-driven policing.
theme_4_justification: Tangential mention: discusses spatial inequality via neighborhood-level predictive policing (p. 108-109) and 'net widening' but not spatial destruction, domicide, or urbicide. No discussion of military urbanism or home unmaking.
key_quotes: Rather than eliminating human discretion, big data is a form of capital, both a social product and a social resource. For that reason alone, big data cannot possibly obviate inequality: like other forms of capital, it is transactional, some people and groups have more of it than others, and it can be extracted from already disadvantaged populations.
Human judgment is hidden in the black box under a patina of objectivity.
When new technology is overlaid onto an old organizational structure, long-standing problems shape themselves to the contours of the new technology.
policy_relevance: Recommends transparency, community engagement, accountability from tech companies, ongoing validation of algorithms, and using big data to target services not just punishment.
notes: Chapter from edited volume 'Predict and Surveil'; focuses on policing inequality in US cities; no explicit military dual-use discussion.
